answer: According to the Commission's draft guidance on high-risk classification, AI systems used to monitor and control critical infrastructure such as power supply, including spotting unusual patterns in grid operating data to help steer functions like load distribution and system stability, are considered high-risk. Therefore, your model falls within the high-risk power-supply category as described in the draft guidelines.

According to the Commission's draft guidance on high-risk classification, a model that predicts power-balance deviations for every quarter hour to help plan system operation is treated as high-risk in the critical-infrastructure category, as it relates to the operation of energy networks which are critical infrastructures.

According to the Commission's draft guidance, an AI tool that predicts a power cut and flags it to the control room, serving as one of several layers of protection with human decision-making following, would be considered a safety-relevant part and thus high-risk, as it contributes to the safety function even if it is not the sole control mechanism. This interpretation comes from the draft guidelines on classification of high-risk AI systems.

According to the Commission's draft guidance on high-risk classification, monitoring data links of a power network for hackers or malicious code is considered part of critical infrastructure protection and thus falls within the high-risk category for critical infrastructure AI systems.
Yes, AI systems intended to be used in the management and operation of critical infrastructure, such as power generation from a reactor, are classified as high-risk under the AI Act.

According to the Commission's draft guidance on high-risk classification, a safety-relevant AI part in the critical-infrastructure category is not automatically high-risk whenever any Distribution System Operator (DSO) uses it; the DSO's status matters for the classification.

Yes, as a municipal power network operator governed by public law using a high-risk AI system in the critical-infrastructure category, you must assess its impact on fundamental rights before use, since the AI Act requires conformity assessment and risk management for high-risk AI systems, which includes consideration of fundamental rights implications.
A high-risk AI system from the critical-infrastructure category must be registered in the EU database for high-risk AI systems to be officially on record.
After the 2026 changes, the high-risk requirements in Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3 start applying to AI systems classified as high-risk because their use falls under Annex III from 1 January 2027.

No, the need for third-party conformity assessment solely due to radio-frequency use or electromagnetic interference that does not affect health or safety does not meet the Article 6(1)(b) test for being high-risk under the AI Act.

A part is considered to be doing a safety job if it is intended to directly or indirectly fulfill a safety function, meaning it contributes to the safe operation of the AI system by preventing or mitigating risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights. This includes parts that are essential for the AI system to perform safety-related tasks as defined in the AI Act's context of safety-relevant parts.

From 2026, users of high-risk AI systems have an obligation to use the system according to the instructions and ensure that persons under their authority have appropriate knowledge and skills to use the system safely and in compliance with the regulation.

No, requiring a person to review every result alone is not sufficient to remove a system in an Annex III use area from the high-risk category. The AI Act classifies systems based on their intended use and risk, and human oversight requirements do not by themselves change the classification.

The presence of a separate fallback safeguard on the power network does not affect whether the AI tool itself is considered a safety-relevant part of the network under the AI Act. The classification depends on the AI tool's role and impact on safety, not on external fallback measures.

As a TSO using a high-risk AI system, you must keep the logs and records generated by the AI system under your control for at least 5 years after the AI system has been placed on the market or put into service.

According to the Commission's draft guidelines on the definition of an AI system, an AI system is software that is developed with one or more techniques and approaches listed in the AI Act and can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, generate outputs such as content, predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing the environments they interact with. Using a trained model solely to speed up a well-proven first-principles model by calculating its coefficients may not qualify as an AI system if the software does not generate outputs as described or does not use the AI techniques listed. However, the draft guidelines do not explicitly address this specific scenario, so interpretation may vary.

According to the Commission's draft guidance, an AI tool that only makes critical infrastructure cheaper or more efficient to operate does not count as a safety component in the high-risk critical-infrastructure category, as the focus is on safety-related functions rather than economic efficiency.

As a TSO officially designated as a critical entity, your AI systems used for security purposes such as video, radar, and UAVs to guard fences around substations are classified as high-risk AI systems under the AI Act. You must comply with the high-risk requirements from the date the AI Act enters into application, which is 18 months after its entry into force.

After the 2026 changes, the EU law for machines is listed in Annex I(B) of the AI Act. For a high-risk AI system acting as a safety-relevant part of a machine, the requirements of Title III (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity) apply, as specified for high-risk AI systems under the AI Act.

The provider of a high-risk AI system must report any serious incident, such as a severe disruption of electricity-grid operation that cannot be reversed, to the relevant authorities without undue delay and no later than 15 calendar days after becoming aware of the incident.

Under the amended AI Act, high-risk AI systems that were placed on the market or put into service before the date of application of the regulation are not subject to the high-risk requirements unless they are substantially modified after that date. The cut-off date is the date of application of the regulation, which is 17 July 2024. Since your high-risk AI tool went live in 2025, after the cut-off date, it is subject to the high-risk rules even if you plan to leave it essentially as it is.

If you have concluded under Article 6(3) that your Annex III grid AI tool is not high-risk, you must still comply with the transparency obligations applicable to AI systems listed in Annex III before first making it available on the EU market.

According to the Commission's draft guidance on high-risk classification, AI used in fire detection and warning systems for critical entities like a cloud hosting facility is considered high-risk. Therefore, the supplier must have the system undergo conformity assessment by an external certification body before placing it on the market.
